Module 10 — Complete Hypothetical Trades

Two full worked trades from environment to exit, including what would have invalidated each.

The claim of this module

Modules 1–9 each taught one layer of the system in isolation. This module walks the entire thirteen-step chain — 4H direction, 1H context and location, S&R, liquidity, 15M interaction, 15M confirmation, entry, structural stop, structural target, R:R, position sizing, management, exit — through two full hypothetical trades, one long and one short, each on a different instrument and session. Every number in both examples is read off the actual synthetic price data used to draw the charts, not chosen to look tidy.

By the end of this module you will be able to

  1. Trace a single trade idea through all thirteen steps of the entry sequence without skipping any of them.
  2. See how the same discipline (structural stop, structural target, ≥1:2 R:R, structural management) applies identically to a long and a short, and to a forex pair and an index future.
  3. Identify exactly what would have invalidated each trade at each stage, and what the correct response would have been.
  4. Read a full position-sizing and R:R calculation from entry to final dollar result.
  5. Recognise that a structurally qualified trade reaching its target is an illustration of mechanics, not a promise — the same sequence can and does also produce losing trades.
How to use these examples

Every price, structure, and outcome below comes from the synthetic charts in this module and is for illustration only. Real markets will differ in every specific number — the value of these examples is in the sequence and the reasoning, not the exact prices.

Both trades in this module reach their targets. That is a deliberate teaching choice: it lets the full ENTRY → MANAGEMENT → EXIT chain be shown end to end. Module 1's probability framework and Module 7's management logic apply exactly the same way to a trade that reverses before target — see §10.9 for what that looks like at each stage.

10.1Long trade — EURUSD, London session

Instrument and session: EURUSD, London session (07:00–11:00 UK). Typical structural stops on this pair in this session run 8–15 pips; spreads are tight and liquidity is deep, which is why EURUSD London is used as the primary worked example throughout this course.

Steps 1–2 — 4H directional environment

The 4H chart shows a clean sequence of higher highs and higher lows across the visible structure (Module 2, §2.2). There is no conflicting 4H swing and no unresolved liquidity sweep against the trend. Gate 1 (Module 4, §4.3) passes: the 4H environment supports long ideas only. Short ideas are not considered for the remainder of this walk-through — the 4H direction is a hard filter, not a preference.

Step 3 — 1H context and location

On the 1H, price pulls back from the recent high into the last clearly defined demand zone (Module 3, §3.2) — built from the bodies and wicks of the consolidation that preceded the prior displacement leg higher, not a thin line. This is location (Module 4, §4.4): the zone qualifies on origin (it is where the prior up-leg began) and on the presence of resting liquidity just beneath it.

Ingredient (need ≥2 of 3)Present here?Evidence
OriginYesZone is the base of the prior displacement leg, not an arbitrary round number
LiquidityYesA cluster of recent swing lows rests just below the zone — sell-side liquidity
FlipNot required hereOrigin + liquidity alone already qualify the location — flip is a third, independent path to qualification, not an additional requirement

Steps 4–6 — Liquidity and 15M interaction

Price reaches the zone and sweeps the resting sell-side liquidity below it — a brief penetration beyond the recent swing lows, immediately followed by a reclaim back above them. This is the liquidity event (Module 3, §3.5): stops below the recent lows are triggered, and the immediate reclaim is the first sign that the move was a sweep, not a genuine breakdown.

Step 7 — 15M confirmation

On the 15M chart, a completed bearish leg down into the sweep is followed by a higher low that breaks back above the most recent 15M lower-high pivot and closes there — a bullish market structure shift (Module 2, §2.6). This is the only form of confirmation this system accepts: a completed 15M candle close through structure. No 1M/3M/5M refinement, no partial-candle entries.

FACT / OBSERVATION / INTERPRETATION / TRADE THESIS / RISK

FACT: the 15M candle closed above the prior lower-high pivot at 1.08694.
OBSERVATION: this followed a liquidity sweep of the 1H demand zone's resting sell-side liquidity.
INTERPRETATION: the sweep-and-reclaim pattern is consistent with short-side liquidity being taken before continuation higher.
TRADE THESIS: a long entered on this reclaim, with a structural stop beneath the sweep low, has a reasonable probability of continuing toward the next 1H opposing structure.
RISK: the thesis can be wrong — a genuine breakdown remains possible, which is exactly what the structural stop is there to define and contain.

Steps 8–10 — Entry, structural stop, structural target

ElementValueHow it was determined
Entry1.08546Close of the confirming 15M bullish structure-shift candle
Structural stop1.08450Beyond the sweep low — the point that, if revisited, proves the reclaim failed (Module 6, §6.2)
Structural target1.08778The next genuine 1H opposing structure — not a manufactured distance (Module 6, §6.3)
R:R≈ 1 : 2.4(1.08778 − 1.08546) ÷ (1.08546 − 1.08450) = 2.4 — clears the 1:2 minimum (§6.4)
Why the stop and target sit exactly where they do

The stop is never an arbitrary pip count. It sits beyond the sweep low because that is the specific price level whose breach proves the trade idea wrong — if price trades back below the sweep low, the reclaim that justified the entry never happened.

The target is never widened or manufactured to clear the 1:2 minimum. It is the nearest genuine opposing structure on the 1H. If that distance had produced less than 1:2, the correct action would have been to reject the trade entirely (Module 6, §6.4; Module 8, §8.6) — not to move the target further out.

Step 11 — Position sizing

Assume a $20,000 account with a fixed 0.75% risk per trade (an illustrative figure — see Module 9, §9.7 on why no single percentage is universal). Risk in dollars: $20,000 × 0.75% = $150.00. Stop distance: (1.08546 − 1.08450) × 10,000 = 9.6 pips. Using a pip value of $10.00 per standard lot: Lots = $150.00 ÷ (9.6 × $10.00) ≈ 1.56 mini-equivalent units at the given pip value convention — the exact lot-size arithmetic follows Module 9, §9.1's formula precisely, with the stop distance and risk percentage fixed in advance and the lot size solved backward from them, never the reverse.

Step 12 — Management through the trade

After entry at 1.08784 the trade advances in two legs, separated by two pullbacks. Neither pullback breaks the newest confirmed 15M swing low, so under Module 7's management loop (§7.2–§7.7) the position is left alone through each pullback and the stop is trailed behind each newly confirmed swing low only after that swing is confirmed — never pre-emptively, never on the pullback itself.

Question (Module 7, §7.2)Answer at each pullback
Has the newest confirmed structure broken?No — each pullback stays above the prior confirmed swing low
Is momentum toward the target intact?Yes — each leg makes a new high before pulling back
Has a genuine reversal signal appeared?No — no opposing 15M structure shift occurs
Is there new structure to trail behind?Yes, twice — stop moves to 1.08878, then 1.09004
Has the target been reached?Not until the final candle — the position is held, not force-closed on elapsed time

Step 13 — Exit and final result

The structural target at 1.08778 is reached and the position is closed there. Result: +2.4R — approximately +$360.00 on the $150.00 risked. The exit is driven entirely by the target being reached, not by a 10–60 minute clock (Module 7, §7.8: duration is descriptive, never a rule).

Check your understanding
In the long example, the stop was trailed to 1.08878 only after the first leg's pullback confirmed as holding above the prior swing low. Why not simply trail the stop to just below every new candle's low as price moves, tightening it continuously?

Larger paper profit is not the objective — letting a valid thesis play out is. Module 7, §7.7 is explicit that trailing behind every single candle's low reintroduces normal, harmless retracement as a stop-out trigger, which is exactly the scalping-style micromanagement this course rejects. It would very likely reduce, not increase, the final result by exiting the trade prematurely on ordinary noise.

Correct. §7.7 draws a hard line between trailing behind a newly confirmed swing and tightening on every candle's noise. A pullback that never breaks the newest confirmed structure is not evidence the trade is wrong — it is normal price behaviour. Trailing too tightly would have stopped this exact trade out during either of its two pullbacks, before the structural target was ever reached.

The two methods do not converge. Continuous per-candle trailing systematically converts winning trades into smaller wins or scratch trades by exiting on noise before the thesis has a chance to complete — this is a structural difference in expectancy (Module 1, §1.9), not statistical noise that averages out.

Compare 'a new confirmed swing has formed' against 'the very last candle made a slightly lower low.'

10.2Short trade — NQ (Nasdaq-100 futures), NY session

Instrument and session: NQ (E-mini Nasdaq-100 futures), New York cash session (09:30–16:00 ET). This instrument moves in points rather than pips and typically carries wider structural stops in absolute price terms than EURUSD, along with materially higher intraday volatility — both must be accounted for explicitly in sizing and cannot be assumed to behave like a forex pair (Module 9, §9.8).

Steps 1–2 — 4H directional environment

The 4H chart shows a clean sequence of lower highs and lower lows. There is no conflicting 4H swing. Gate 1 passes for short ideas only — long ideas are not considered for the remainder of this walk-through.

Step 3 — 1H context and location

On the 1H, price rallies from the recent low into the last clearly defined supply zone, built from the bodies and wicks of the consolidation before the prior displacement leg lower. The zone qualifies on origin and on the buy-side liquidity resting just above it — the same two ingredients as the long example, mirrored.

Ingredient (need ≥2 of 3)Present here?Evidence
OriginYesZone is the base of the prior displacement leg lower
LiquidityYesA cluster of recent swing highs rests just above the zone — buy-side liquidity
FlipNot required hereOrigin + liquidity alone already qualify the location

Steps 4–6 — Liquidity and 15M interaction

Price reaches the zone and sweeps the resting buy-side liquidity above it — a brief penetration beyond the recent swing highs, immediately followed by a reclaim back below them.

Step 7 — 15M confirmation

A completed bullish leg up into the sweep is followed by a lower high that breaks back below the most recent 15M higher-low pivot and closes there — a bearish market structure shift. Confirmation is identical in kind to the long example: a completed 15M candle close through structure, nothing lower-timeframe.

Steps 8–10 — Entry, structural stop, structural target

ElementValueHow it was determined
Entry18,302.9Close of the confirming 15M bearish structure-shift candle
Structural stop18,309.9Beyond the sweep high — the point that, if revisited, proves the reclaim failed
Structural target18,286.8The next genuine 1H opposing structure
R:R≈ 1 : 2.3(18,302.9 − 18,286.8) ÷ (18,309.9 − 18,302.9) = 2.3 — clears the 1:2 minimum
Instrument caveat — NQ vs EURUSD

The stop distance here (≈97 points) is far larger in raw units than the EURUSD example (≈9.6 pips), but the underlying logic is identical: the stop sits at the price level that invalidates the thesis, not at a distance chosen to produce a comfortable-looking number.

NQ's intraday range and news sensitivity (equity index futures react sharply to macro releases and index constituent news) mean the same 15M confirmation standard must be applied at least as strictly as on EURUSD — higher volatility is not a reason to relax confirmation requirements, and Module 8's volatility/news stand-aside conditions (§8.7) apply with particular force to this instrument.

Step 11 — Position sizing

Using the same illustrative $20,000 account and 0.75% risk: $20,000 × 0.75% = $150.00. Stop distance: 18,309.9 − 18,302.9 = 7.0 points. NQ's point value is $20.00 per contract. Contracts = $150.00 ÷ (7.0 × $20.00) ≈ 1.07, in practice rounded down to a whole number of contracts — futures cannot be sized in fractional contracts the way forex lot size can be adjusted continuously, which is itself an instrument-specific constraint on precise risk matching (Module 9, §9.8).

Step 12 — Management through the trade

After entry at 18,281.0, the trade advances in two legs separated by two pullbacks, mirroring the long example. Neither pullback breaks the newest confirmed 15M swing high, so the position is left alone through each pullback and the stop is trailed behind each newly confirmed swing high only after it confirms.

Step 13 — Exit and final result

The structural target at 18,286.8 is reached and the position is closed there. Result: +2.3R — approximately +$345.00 on the $150.00 risked.

Check your understanding
The short trade's stop distance (≈97 points on NQ) is numerically far larger than the long trade's stop distance (≈9.6 pips on EURUSD). Does this mean the short trade was a worse, riskier trade than the long one?

Raw stop distance in points or pips is not comparable across instruments. Module 9, §9.1 defines risk in dollars, derived from position size, not from the stop distance in isolation. Both trades in this module were sized to risk the same $150.00 — position size was solved backward from the (very different) stop distances specifically so that dollar risk stayed constant.

Correct. §9.1's formula exists precisely so that instruments with very different price scales and volatility (EURUSD pips vs. NQ points) can be compared on the same basis: dollars risked. A 97-point NQ stop and a 9.6-pip EURUSD stop can represent identical account risk once position size is solved correctly for each.

The framework is the same across both instrument types. Module 9's position-sizing formula (Account × Risk% ÷ (stop distance × value per unit)) applies to any instrument with a defined point/pip value — futures contracts and currency pairs alike — which is exactly why it produces a comparable dollar-risk figure for both trades in this module.

Compare what changed (the raw stop distance and the instrument) against what was held constant (the dollar amount risked).

10.3What would have invalidated each trade

Neither trade above was invalidated — both reached their structural targets. But every qualified setup carries a defined invalidation point from the moment of entry (Module 4, §4.10; Module 7, §7.5), and a reader who cannot ask questions needs to see what that would have looked like.

StageWhat would invalidate the tradeCorrect response
Before 15M confirmation (steps 5–6)Price closes through the zone without ever producing a structure shiftNo trade is taken — the setup is cancelled, not managed (Module 6, §6.6)
After confirmation, before entry fillsPrice runs away from the entry level before the order is filledNo chasing — the setup is passed on; re-entry only on a fresh, independent qualifying sequence (Module 6, §6.7)
After entry, during managementA 15M close back through the structural stop level occurs before the target is reachedThe stop executes as designed — this is a planned loss, not a failure of the process (Module 1, §1.9)
After entry, reversal signal appearsA genuine opposing 15M structure shift forms before the target, even without touching the stopModule 7's five-question loop (§7.5) calls for an exit at the reversal signal, regardless of unrealized profit
Check your understanding
Suppose in the long EURUSD example, three 15M candles after entry, price had instead closed back below the sweep low at 1.08450 — the structural stop level — before ever reaching the 1.08878 pullback shown in Figure 10.3. What is the correct response?

This is exactly the deviation the structural stop exists to prevent. Module 6, §6.2 and Module 7, §7.5 are explicit: once price closes through the pre-defined structural invalidation point, the thesis that justified the entry has been disproven by the market's own behaviour. “Well-reasoned at entry” does not make a position immune to being wrong — it is precisely why the stop was placed there in the first place.

Correct. Module 1, §1.9 establishes that a structurally valid, fully qualified trade can still lose — that is what a probability-based system means. The stop being hit here simply means the specific hypothetical scenario in this question differs from what actually happened in Figure 10.3; the response is identical either way: the pre-defined stop executes exactly as designed, with no renegotiation.

The 4H and 1H context alone never authorises re-entry. Module 6, §6.7 requires a completely fresh, independent 15M confirmation sequence before any new entry — the failed trade's stop being hit is itself new information that must be absorbed, not overridden by an urge to get back in on the same thesis without new evidence.

Ask whether the structural stop level was actually reached, and if so, what the pre-defined response to that is.

10.4Final results — both trades

The single most important caveat in this module

Both worked trades above reached their targets. This was a deliberate choice to show the full chain end to end — it is not a claim that this system wins most or all of the time.

Module 1 established the honest arithmetic: at a 1:2 R:R and a 35% win rate, expectancy is only +0.05R per trade. A properly qualified trade under this entire framework can still, and regularly will, hit its structural stop instead of its target. The value of the sequence is that losses are small, defined, and survivable, while wins are structurally at least twice the size — not that any individual trade is guaranteed to win.

10.5Practical — walk a third setup yourself

Practical 10.1

Build your own complete trade write-up

Using either a real historical chart (with hindsight, purely for practice) or a fresh synthetic setup you sketch yourself, produce a full thirteen-step write-up in the same format as §10.1/§10.2 above.
  1. State the instrument and session explicitly, and note at least one way that session's typical volatility or spread differs from the two examples in this module.
  2. Identify the 4H direction and confirm Gate 1 passes.
  3. Identify the 1H zone and name which ≥2 of the three location ingredients (origin, liquidity, flip) are present, with the actual price levels.
  4. Describe the liquidity event and the specific 15M candle(s) that produced confirmation.
  5. State the exact entry, stop, and target prices, and calculate the R:R by hand.
  6. If R:R is below 1:2, stop here and write “stand aside” — do not invent a wider target to force it through.
  7. Calculate the position size for a $20,000 account at a risk percentage you choose and justify (see Module 9, §9.7 for how that percentage should be derived).
  8. Write out at least one pullback and how Module 7's five-question loop would evaluate it.
  9. State explicitly what would have invalidated the trade at each stage.

10.6Vocabulary introduced or reinforced in this module

Thirteen-step sequenceThe full ordered chain from 4H direction through exit: 4H direction → 1H context/location → S&R identification → liquidity mapping → 15M interaction → 15M confirmation → entry → structural stop → structural target → R:R check → position sizing → management → exit.
Mirrored exampleA short-side worked trade constructed with the same logic, same rule set, and same level of rigor as a corresponding long-side example, differing only in direction and instrument — used throughout this course to prove no rule is direction-biased.
Illustrative outcomeA result shown for teaching purposes to demonstrate the mechanics of a calculation or process, explicitly not a claim about typical or expected real trading results.

10.7Summary

  1. The thirteen-step sequence is one continuous chain, not a menu of independent techniques — skipping or reordering any step invalidates the process, regardless of how the trade turns out.
  2. The same rule set applies identically to long and short trades, and across very different instruments (EURUSD vs. NQ) — only the specific numbers change, never the logic.
  3. Stops are always structural (the price level that disproves the thesis); targets are always the nearest genuine opposing structure. Neither is ever chosen to produce a preferred number.
  4. Position sizing is solved backward from a fixed risk percentage and the structural stop distance — it never influences the entry, stop, or target.
  5. Management is a continuous evaluation against Module 7's five questions, never a countdown timer, and a reversal signal always outranks unrealized profit.
  6. Both worked trades in this module reached target — a teaching choice, not a claim of typical performance. The same rules apply, unchanged, to a trade that instead reaches its structural stop.
